title: Quoting Accurately from Texts
keyIdea: A quotation is the writer's exact words, copied word for word and put inside quotation marks. Quote only the words that prove your point, whether the text says it outright or gives a clue you infer from. Lead in with a signal phrase such as "According to the text," and then explain what the quotation shows.

kid: When you write about a text, you can prove your point with its own words. That is a quotation. Copy the words exactly, then put quotation marks round them. Your own words stay outside the marks.
Quote just the words that prove your point. To show Mia was nervous, "Her hands shook" is enough. A whole paragraph hides your proof, and one word on its own may not make sense.
Check your copy word by word. "Her hand was shaking" is not what the story says, even if it means the same. Changing a word, an ending or a small word like "her" turns a quote into a misquote.

Texts do not always say things outright. The story never says Mia was proud, but "Mia grinned all the way home" is a clue. Quote the clue, then say what it shows. Start with a signal phrase, such as "According to the text,".
adult: This reading skill (ages 10 to 11, Common Core RL.5.1 and RI.5.1) asks learners to quote accurately from literary and informational texts, both for what a text says explicitly and for inferences. In practice that means choosing relevant words, copying them exactly and punctuating them as a quotation.

Good quotations are short and relevant: a phrase or sentence that proves one point. They are introduced with a signal phrase ("The author states", "According to the text") and followed by an explanation that links the words to the claim. Copied words go inside quotation marks; the learner's own wording stays outside.

Common mistakes: copying a long passage instead of the proving words; paraphrasing but still using quotation marks; changing small words or endings (hand for hands, the for her); quoting accurate words that do not support the claim; and dropping a quotation in with no signal phrase or explanation.

In the lab, learners drag across a story to select proof for a claim, spot the three changes in a classmate's misquote, tap gaps to place opening and closing marks, quote a clue for an inference, and build a signal phrase, quotation and explanation from tiles. The challenge uses a new non-fiction text about honeybees.

familyTip: When your child tells you a book character is mean or brave, ask, "Which words in the book tell you that?" Let them find the exact words and read them out, then say what those words show.

practice.prompt: The story says: "Tom slammed the door and stomped up the stairs." Which quote best proves Tom was angry?
practice.hint: Which words show how Tom acted? Are they the story's own words?
practice.explain: "slammed the door and stomped" is copied exactly and shows anger. "up the stairs" does not show a feeling, and the story never says "Tom was very cross".

practice.prompt: A quote you want to use has {a} words, but only the last {b} prove your point. How many words should you quote?
practice.hint: Quote only the words that do the proving.
practice.explain: Quote just the {b} words that prove the point. The other words only hide your proof.

practice.prompt: The text says: "The river was wide and brown." Which is an accurate quote?
choices: The text says the river "was wide and brown."
The text says the river "was big and brown."
The text says the river "is wide and brown."
practice.hint: Compare each word with the text, one at a time.
practice.explain: Only "was wide and brown" matches exactly. "big" changes a word, and "is" changes the ending of the verb.

practice.prompt: Sam's sentence has {a} words. Only {b} of them are copied from the text. How many words go inside the quotation marks?
practice.hint: Only copied words go inside the marks. Your own words stay outside.
practice.explain: The {b} copied words go inside the marks. The other words are Sam's own, so they stay outside.

practice.prompt: Which is a signal phrase that leads in to a quotation?
practice.hint: A signal phrase points the reader to the text, not to you.
practice.explain: "According to the text," tells the reader the next words come from the text. The other two lead in to your own opinion.

pool.prompt: What must be true of the words inside quotation marks?
choices: They are exactly the writer's words
They mean the same as the writer's words
They are the most important words in the text
pool.hint: Quotation marks make a promise to the reader. What is it?
pool.explain: Quotation marks promise the writer's exact words. Words that only mean the same are a paraphrase, so they go outside the marks.

pool.prompt: The text says: "Ana hid her face and would not speak." Which quote best proves Ana was shy?
choices: "hid her face and would not speak"
pool.hint: Find the copied words that show the feeling.
pool.explain: "hid her face and would not speak" is exact and proves it. One name proves nothing, and the text never says "Ana was shy and quiet".

pool.prompt: The text never says "Leo was hungry". Which quote could prove it?
choices: "Leo's tummy rumbled as he stared at the cake"
pool.hint: You can quote a clue and infer the feeling from it.
pool.explain: A rumbling tummy and staring at cake are clues that let you infer hunger. You cannot quote words the text never uses.

pool.prompt: The text says: "She ran as fast as the wind." Kim writes: She "ran as quick as the wind." What is wrong?
pool.hint: Compare Kim's words with the text one at a time.
pool.explain: "quick" is not the writer's word. Even when the meaning stays the same, a changed word makes it a misquote.

pool.prompt: Where do the quotation marks go in: The poet says the sea was "grey and cold" that morning?
choices: Round only the copied words "grey and cold"
pool.hint: Which words were copied from the poem?
pool.explain: Only "grey and cold" came from the poem, so only those words go inside the marks. The rest is your own sentence.

pool.prompt: What should usually come after a quotation in your answer?
choices: A few words that say what it shows
pool.hint: How will the reader know why you chose those words?
pool.explain: Explaining what the quote shows links it to your point, for example "which shows that Mia was nervous".

pool.prompt: Max copies a {a}-word sentence but changes {b} of the words. How many words does he need to fix to quote it accurately?
pool.hint: An accurate quote has every word exactly as the writer wrote it.
pool.explain: All {b} changed words must go back to the writer's words. One changed word is enough to make a misquote.

pool.prompt: An article says: "Owls can turn their heads a long way round." Which quote proves owls can see behind them?
choices: "Owls can turn their heads a long way round"
pool.hint: Choose words that are really in the article and that support the point.
pool.explain: Turning the head a long way round is the clue. The article never says "see behind their backs", and "Owls are birds" is not in it.

pool.prompt: Your answer quotes {a} separate phrases from the text. How many opening quotation marks (“) does it need?
pool.hint: Each quoted phrase needs its own pair of marks: one to open and one to close.
pool.explain: Each of the {a} phrases opens with its own “ mark, so you need {a} opening marks, and {a} closing marks too.

visual.caption: The story says: "Her hands shook as she held her poem." Is each one an accurate quote? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: drag across a story to quote the proof, spot a misquote, place quotation marks, quote a clue and build a signal phrase, quote and explanation.
